evidence_base.sufficiency_note: 17 sessions across nine months and six subject areas is enough breadth and duration to support a genuine profile, including which patterns are habitual versus one-off.

cognitive_types.label: Fluency
cognitive_types.definition: Retrieving or recalling known material fast and automatically
cognitive_types.summary: Shows up as deliberate self-testing before an exam, where she catches and reverses her own error rather than just re-reading -- but this happens once in the whole corpus.

snippets.subject: Social Studies

preceding_ai_turn.text: Check the order again -- which one would need to happen first for the other to make sense as a reaction?

student_turn.text: wait no, that's backwards, the tariff thing came before, that's literally what South Carolina was reacting to. I had it flipped.

snippets.why: She retrieves a fact, tests it against the logic of the situation, and corrects herself without being told the answer.

cognitive_types.label: Procedural
cognitive_types.definition: Executing a known sequence correctly, step by step
cognitive_types.summary: Reliable across math and computer science homework -- she debugs and corrects her own execution more often than she asks to be told the fix.

snippets.subject: Computer Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: And what is `current` set to right before the loop starts?

student_turn.text: oh wait. I never actually initialized current before the loop, it's just... nothing. that's probably it.

snippets.why: She locates her own bug from a guiding question rather than being handed the fix.

snippets.subject: Mathematics

preceding_ai_turn.text: Try taking the log of both sides first.

student_turn.text: ok, log(3^(x+1)) = log(5^x), so (x+1)log3 = x log5. then... x log3 + log3 = x log5. x log3 - x log5 = -log3. x(log3 - log5) = -log3. x = -log3 / (log3 - log5).

snippets.why: Full independent execution of an unfamiliar problem type, then self-checked by estimation two turns later.

cognitive_types.label: Conceptual
cognitive_types.definition: Building or repairing a mental model of how something works
cognitive_types.summary: Her clearest strength when a task lets her build something rather than just apply it -- most visible in a session where she catches and repairs a wrong mental model of logarithms in real time.

snippets.subject: Mathematics

preceding_ai_turn.text: That's division, not what a log is asking. A log answers: what power do I raise the base to, to get this number?

student_turn.text: OH. it's not division at all, it's asking what power. so log is literally just 'the exponent' dressed up.

snippets.why: A wrong model (log as division) is named, confronted, and replaced with a correct one in her own words -- the clearest sign of structural understanding rather than memorization.

snippets.subject: Computer Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: For some structures a loop doesn't map cleanly onto the shape of the problem -- like anything nested to an unknown depth.

student_turn.text: wait so for something like a file system with folders inside folders a loop wouldn't even really work the same way right, because you don't know how deep it goes

snippets.why: She generates her own example that tests the boundary of the new concept, unprompted.

cognitive_types.label: Critical Thinking
cognitive_types.definition: Evaluating, reasoning about, or challenging a claim
cognitive_types.summary: Consistently strong whenever a task asks her to weigh sources or claims against each other -- and she reuses the same reasoning method across two separate assignments months apart.

snippets.subject: Social Studies

preceding_ai_turn.text: So how would you use each?

student_turn.text: my thesis is going to be that personal accounts show the human cost even when the official numbers look good, so you need both, not that one is right

snippets.why: A synthesized thesis built on a reasoning principle about source reliability, not a side picked in advance.

snippets.subject: English

preceding_ai_turn.text: That's a reasonable claim, but it's also the first thing most readers would say about the yam. What's the more specific or arguable version of that idea, if there is one?

student_turn.text: I guess what's actually interesting is that the yam thing works because it's not really about masculinity, it's about control. he can't control the yam harvest either, that's the whole point of the failed year.

snippets.why: She rejects the obvious reading of her own thesis and builds a sharper, more specific claim.

cognitive_types.label: Creative
cognitive_types.definition: Generating something novel; diverging rather than converging
cognitive_types.summary: Thin in volume but real when it appears -- she sets her own aesthetic standard rather than a correctness standard, and acts on it even though it's riskier.

snippets.subject: Visual Arts

student_turn.text: I want to try something asymmetrical instead of centering it, even though centering is safer

snippets.why: A self-generated creative direction chosen specifically because it's riskier than the safe option, not because it was assigned.

cognitive_types.label: Metacognitive
cognitive_types.definition: Monitoring and regulating their own thinking and learning
cognitive_types.summary: The most frequent type in the transcript by a wide margin -- she narrates her own process constantly, and at its best this becomes precise enough to produce a rule she sets for herself.

snippets.subject: General

preceding_ai_turn.text: If you compare it to the first draft, is it better?

student_turn.text: if I compare it to the first draft it's obviously better. i think the real answer is i'm not actually editing anymore, i'm just checking

snippets.why: She distinguishes two things that feel identical from the inside -- editing versus checking -- and the distinction is her own, not supplied.

snippets.subject: Computer Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: What's actually bothering you about the 94?

student_turn.text: it's not the grade i guess. i said out loud in class it was the worst thing i'd turned in and then i got a 94 on it and now i don't know if i actually think that or if i was just performing being hard on myself

snippets.why: She catches herself performing self-criticism as a hedge against disappointment -- an unusually precise piece of self-observation.

cognitive_types.label: Transfer
cognitive_types.definition: Applying something known to a genuinely different context
cognitive_types.summary: Rare -- one instance in the whole corpus -- but fully realized: she names the same skepticism she applies to historical sources as the thing she should apply to the tutor's own claims.

snippets.subject: Social Studies

preceding_ai_turn.text: That's a strong, synthesized thesis -- and it's the same method you used on the practice documents in January.

student_turn.text: yeah I remembered that conversation actually. glad i didn't have to relearn it. it's kind of the same thing as when I don't just believe whatever you tell me either, right, same idea but with documents instead of you

snippets.why: She independently recognizes that 'evaluate a source's incentive to distort' is the same move whether the source is a historical document or the AI tutor itself -- a genuinely different context, and she made the connection, not the tutor.

cognitive_types.label: Exploratory
cognitive_types.definition: Encountering new information and taking it in
cognitive_types.summary: Almost absent as its own category -- when she encounters new material she tends to move quickly into building or applying it rather than staying in intake mode.

snippets.subject: Computer Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: A recursive function is one that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem until it hits a base case. Loops repeat; recursion breaks a problem into smaller copies of itself.

student_turn.text: ok so is it ever actually better or just a different way to write the same thing

snippets.why: A follow-up in a direction she chose, before the turn immediately after tips into genuine Conceptual work.

offloading.summary: All three instances are narrow and low-stakes -- she hands off routine verification or arithmetic, never the core reasoning of an assignment. The more notable pattern in this corpus isn't task offloading; it's reassurance-seeking, where she asks the tutor to render a verdict ('is a 94 bad', 'is this an A thesis') on work she has already done herself. Twice, the tutor declined to hand over writing she asked for outright (T101, a paragraph rewrite), and both times she completed the work herself afterward.

instances.subject: Mathematics

student_turn.text: ok I rewrote it: angle A = angle D, angle C = angle F (both right angles, given), AC = DF (given), so ASA, so triangle ABC = triangle DEF. can you just check the whole thing this time so I'm not up all night.

instances.note: She had already done the actual reasoning and rewrite herself; this hands off only the final verification, a reasonable trade at midnight.

instances.subject: Computer Science

student_turn.text: Can you just look at the whole file, I want to make sure there's nothing else weird before I submit.

instances.note: Requested after she had already found and fixed two bugs herself; the request produced a real catch (an empty-list edge case) that she then reasoned through herself.

instances.subject: Mathematics

student_turn.text: I don't want to do math at 1am wrong, can you just calculate it. current average is 96.2, this exam is 20% of the grade.

instances.note: A one-off grade-average calculation handed over outright; nothing about the result changed how she felt about it.

teacher_actions.action: When she asks a yes/no reassurance question ('is a 94 bad', 'is this good enough'), turn it back on her before answering -- 'what do you think, looking at it again' -- rather than supplying the verdict.
teacher_actions.rationale: The single sharpest self-insight in the whole corpus (T121-123, recognizing she performs self-criticism as a hedge) happened because the tutor asked that question instead of just answering hers.

teacher_actions.action: Ask her directly, roughly monthly, where a method from one class shows up in another.
teacher_actions.rationale: She made this connection once, completely unprompted, months apart (source-reliability reasoning in January reused for a real DBQ in April, and extended to how she treats the tutor's own claims) -- it cost her nothing to produce and it's a proven capability, not yet a habit.

teacher_actions.action: Point her at the syllabus grade calculator instead of the tutor for 'what does this score do to my average' questions.
teacher_actions.rationale: These are the lowest-value exchanges in the transcript by her own account ('why does that not make me feel better') -- late-night arithmetic that produces no learning and doesn't touch the actual worry.

teacher_actions.action: Name the exhibition-piece pattern to her directly: noticing she rejected a correct, safe choice for a riskier, more original one.
teacher_actions.rationale: She may not recognize this as a strength given how much of her other work is graded on correctness -- naming it protects a pattern that's currently invisible to her as anything other than extra effort.

caveats: This is one tool on one platform across one school year -- it doesn't capture in-class work, paper homework, tests, or conversations with teachers and peers.

The sessions here are self-selected: she brought these conversations to an AI tutor, usually late at night and usually because something was due or she was anxious about it, which skews the sample away from whatever she does easily without help.
Depth ratings reflect what she wrote in the moment, not independently verified retention or understanding.
All data in this analysis is synthetic, generated for a product demonstration.
